name: Product Pricing

claims.claim_text: A vendor whose business is not hobbyist supply can hold a development board at a high price simply because the hobbyist segment is not a market it cares to serve.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's because that's not their business. They don't want it to be their business, so they charge 400 bucks because they can.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: A mass-market children's toy can carry a roughly ten-to-one gap between manufacturing cost and retail price, with a few dollars of parts sold for tens of dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: it probably cost them, like, you know, $4 to make and they charge parents, like, 50 bucks for it
claims.episode_title: Callow Cough Coverups

claims.claim_text: A crowdfunding pledge tier that includes both a finished electromechanical product and shipping for about twenty dollars is a signal that the campaign's unit economics do not close.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think you can manufacture such a system so cheap and afford to ship it to people for 20 bucks
claims.episode_title: Multicopter, DIY drones & Tektronix - Zappy Zendik Zoilism

claims.claim_text: HDMI became cheap enough to implement in hardware that a small Linux single-board computer could plausibly hit a $25 retail price, albeit on very thin margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: the HDMI doesn't cost you much on the hardware side these days to actually implement that. So, yeah, really, I can't see why they can't do it for $25.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: Early bright LEDs were priced at around a dollar into indicator applications even though the incumbent market had been paying roughly $70 per part, a deliberate choice to open a volume segment rather than harvest the old price.
claims.quote_verbatim: Was there a temptation to sell it for $10 instead of $1 just because you could? Because that's what the market – the market was used to paying $70.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: When a crowdfunded product's claimed feature set (electronics, HD video capture, recording, battery) cannot physically be built into the stated volume at the stated price, the price itself is the tell that it will not ship.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's no way you can produce something, electronics and HD video and recording and battery and everything that small. Not for the price they wanted.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Keeping at least one product in a price range a self-funded hobbyist can afford, even as the higher-end line climbs, brings new users into the ecosystem and the surrounding software.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've tried to, you know, always have, uh, offerings in the, in the, in the range that are reasonable for someone who's a hobbyist
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: A transparent retail price can be built as 2.6 times the bill of materials, a multiplier derived from stacking two 40 percent margins: one for the manufacturer acting as wholesaler and one for the retailer.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's 2.6 times the bill of materials. And that number is based on two 40% margins, one for us, the wholesaler, and one for another 40% margin for the retailers.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Pricing at a bare BOM multiplier with no intellectual-property loading caps how far a copyist can undercut you: they can strip out roughly one of the stacked 40 percent margins and no more.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, the Chinese will underprice us by maybe like one of those 40% margins.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: For consumer accessories, roughly $100 acts as a psychological ceiling below which a large addressable market will buy on impulse.
claims.quote_verbatim: people are trying to target the $100 range or so because it's still, you know, consumer-friendly then
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Customers pay a premium over a cheaper equivalent when the price also buys someone who will diagnose and remove their specific pain, which is why understanding the customer's application matters more than knowing your own equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do you reduce pain for people? And then they'll pay for it.
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Wolke (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: A retail price has to be built up from parts cost, then the distributor's roughly 40 percent margin, then your own margin on top; the resulting number is what the product must sell for.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have to make their 40% margin, right? So we've talked about that before. And then you've got to make your margin on top of that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Announcing a price before the silicon and manufacturing are proven is risky, because failed respins or unexpected costs may force the price up later.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, I don't want anyone to, like, commit us to that price point.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors targeting million-unit sockets deliberately set single-unit pricing high to price small buyers out rather than support them.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want you to buy one of them. They want you to buy one million of them. So, they price you out of it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: A mocked-up, non-functional replica of a hardware product placed in a realistic customer environment lets you run a purchase-decision experiment and vary the offered price point from customer to customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time you bring a customer in, you can change the experiment. So you can offer it at a different price point.
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: Measuring whether customers will actually pay a premium for an expensive feature such as full robotic automation lets you cut engineering scope from the specification before committing engineers to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: by figuring out whether customers actually will pay a price premium for that automation or not, we're able to do a much better job in setting up the specification
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: Charging $20 to $30 for a development kit rather than giving it away filters out people who sign up for anything free and leaves the genuinely interested users.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it stops the tire kickers, but if you make it $20, $30, you know, it stops the tire kickers, but it gets the genuinely interested.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: Building a beginner kit down to the lowest possible price, and selling it as a multi-pack, removes the fear of destroying an expensive board and lowers the barrier to trying surface-mount soldering.
claims.quote_verbatim: how can we make a kit as cheap as possible? So these people who are so scared of soldering SMT that we can just make a three-pack.
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: At small production volumes, a large share of a product's price tracks its shipping weight rather than its electronics content.
claims.quote_verbatim: at some point, a lot of product pricing, at least at our volumes, is how much it weighs
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Pricing a first-generation product at conventional consumer retail margins, rather than at a high low-volume price, tests whether the product is viable in the form it would eventually reach the mass market, at the cost of near-zero profit on the first run.
claims.quote_verbatim: we decided to go with regular retail margins like you would get out of a normal consumer device so that we could present it to the market in about the same form that it would show up in 2015
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Reselling commodity parts leaves margin hostage to supplier pricing and to anyone who can start the same business from a laptop, which is the argument for developing own-brand products.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why I'm so keen about making our own products because you're not beholden to suppliers' prices.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A margin of five to ten dollars per unit over a lifetime volume of only a couple thousand units does not repay the design, prototyping and management effort, so low-volume products need higher margins.
claims.quote_verbatim: you earn, you know, five bucks a unit or 10 bucks a unit or something. It's like, well, and if you're only going to sell a couple of thousand of them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: The cost figure fed into a pricing multiplier should absorb every foreseeable expense including returns, and the resulting number is then multiplied by about 2.5.
claims.quote_verbatim: factor in every possible thing you can think of, even returns and stuff like that and all sorts of stuff. And yeah, multiply it by that 2.5.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: A distributor typically takes around 60 percent margin, so a 2.5x cost multiplier makes the maker's per-unit earnings equal the distributor's; pricing below that multiplier means the distributor earns more per unit than the person who designed the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if you go below that, the distributor will earn more than you do per product.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware has a viability curve below which the campaign price cannot cover production; a project priced under that line goes bankrupt before delivering, even if the founders pay themselves nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's this viability curve, and if you're under the viability curve, you are guaranteed to go bankrupt before you can produce your 3D printers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: For a one-person hardware business the minimum defensible price is BOM times 2.4, with BOM times 3 the safer figure; pricing lower does no favors because the seller cannot deliver and support the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: which at the very least is bomb times 2.4 or safely bomb times 3
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Machines built from many feeders, vision systems and precision motion have a hard cost floor set by their mechanical content, so their price cannot be pushed arbitrarily low.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's one of those things that ultimately can't get pushed too far down in price, you know, because it's a complex thing you've got to do
claims.episode_title: Warming Up To IoT - Tendentious Thermal Tools

claims.claim_text: Deliberately refusing volume price breaks keeps a board at one low price for everyone, which serves education and small production runs but rules out very high volume commercial use.
claims.quote_verbatim: the price breaks just don't work that way with us. You know, it's, it's, it's cheap for everybody, not just some people.
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: After a crowdfunding campaign and its fulfillment run, one hardware product's price was raised from $100 to about $185 per unit to reflect real costs.
claims.quote_verbatim: we made the price go up quite, you know, from a hundred dollars a unit to, I think we went up to like $185 a unit
claims.speaker: Vic Aprea
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: A price must cover far more than the bill of materials: packaging, firmware programming, engineering time and supply-chain work all carry real cost even when they add no visible hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: So packaging and programming and everything else? None of that has any cost to it? It was their decision. It was their time, supply chain, all these things.
claims.episode_title: No More Naming

claims.claim_text: One small-volume machine was offered at $1,600 as a kit and $2,100 assembled, putting a $500 premium on factory assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: 1600 for a kit. 2100 for an assembled unit. Assembled one. Yeah. So, yeah, 500 bucks premium to assemble it.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: A contract design house's first proposal can come back over-engineered with unrequested features at double the target price, requiring the customer to re-specify parts down to hit the price point.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was double the price that I wanted. And, you know, it had features that I didn't ask for
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Product Logistics

claims.claim_text: An early FPGA board with a BOM of $55 to $59 was retailed at $79, well under the company's normal 1.35 multiplier, with the shortfall treated as a marketing expense to seed university users.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think our total bomb cost on that board was something like $55 or $59. And we retailed it for $79.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: A workable launch pattern is to break even on the first expensive low-volume batch to validate the market, then capture the volume efficiencies you skipped as margin on later runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: it makes a lot of sense to basically break even on your first batch, do it the expensive way to validate the market
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Splitting crowdfunding rewards into a limited early-bird tier and a higher-priced later tier both rewards early backers and leaves a small quantity buffer to absorb production failures.
claims.quote_verbatim: I sort of will price the early bird versus non-early bird rewards to have this buffer of small... A smaller quantity as a buffer.
claims.speaker: David Kronstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Minimum order quantities on custom components such as LCD panels can block production entirely: the demo works and customers want it, but the panel cannot be bought below the vendor's minimum panel count.
claims.quote_verbatim: you cannot actually make the product because you haven't ordered that, you know, LCD that you need to minimum order X panels
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: First-time crowdfunding creators systematically underprice, and the standing advice from people who have run campaigns is to double whatever price you first arrived at.
claims.quote_verbatim: just double the price, like, just every time. Just like, if you can, please, just double the price.
claims.speaker: Zach Dunham
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Trying to build one product that covers every use case drives cost past what any reasonable price can support, so narrowing scope is a pricing decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I tried to make an autopilot that does everything, it would be very difficult to provide it for any reasonable price.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Capping the number of units offered in a crowdfunding campaign bounds the production commitment a solo engineer takes on, and pairs with charging enough per unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: he put a cap on how many reward, how many cameras he was going to make, even
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mergers and People Acquisitions

claims.claim_text: A manufacturing partner will raise the agreed unit price each time the specification changes, so late feature changes push a product past its intended cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've increased the price a few times because we've changed a few things. So it's more expensive than originally intended
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Secret Squirrel

claims.claim_text: A product aimed at a $200 retail class can drift out of its price bracket as component sourcing and specification costs creep up during development.
claims.quote_verbatim: my original intention was that it was going to be a $200 retail meter, right? $200 class meter. And then the prices just crept up and up and up.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The EEVblog Sparkgap Generator

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding pressures creators toward a price low enough to attract a crowd and generate momentum, which conflicts with the price needed to cover production.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to price it at a point that's so attractive that you can get lots of backers and get that buzz
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Offering two board variants only makes sense if the cheaper part yields a meaningful price gap; when the lower-capacity device saved only about $3, the second SKU was dropped.
claims.quote_verbatim: the, the lower capacity one was hardly any cheaper than the higher capacity one. So it wasn't really worthwhile to have two different products.
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Chasing the last fraction of a percent of demanding customers can double a product's price, which is a poor trade against serving the mainstream buyer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can double your price to please an extra 0.1% of the market
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ergs Per Second

claims.claim_text: Tooling costs such as injection molds must be amortized into the price from the outset; without a committed volume or purchase orders, selling piece by piece leaves the real per-unit cost unknown.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't have it all priced in the beginning, you could really get yourself screwed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Motivational Speaker

claims.claim_text: Setting a margin as low as 20 percent leaves no room to absorb manufacturing yield loss; an 80 percent yield can wipe out the profit entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: oh, maybe 20% margin at the offset was a bad idea after I had 80% yield
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: There is a dead band in electronics pricing where a product is too expensive to be an impulse buy and too cheap to be a considered professional purchase, roughly around the $150 to $180 mark.
claims.quote_verbatim: things just shouldn't be $180. Like, I just don't understand what that, that shouldn't exist. At least in electronics.
claims.speaker: Pete Staples
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: A simple test board costing about a dollar to make can sustain a $40 price because the price reflects the value of the measurement, not the hardware content.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's 40 bucks for this test. So this board probably costs a dollar, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Feed the Mouse

claims.claim_text: One sensor node's price ladder ran from a 100-unit first run that was largely given away, to about $70 per unit at 500 pieces, to a planned MSRP near $40 at 5,000 to 10,000 units.
claims.quote_verbatim: In the next run, we are doing 500 and that's going to be about 70 bucks.
claims.speaker: Orkhan Amiraslanov
claims.episode_title: Generic Nodes with Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: Hardware sellers should raise prices on a regular cadence, but the do-it-yourself culture resists this and sellers with thin margins do not survive long enough to keep supplying the community.
claims.quote_verbatim: I feel like you've got to raise your prices on a pretty regular basis too.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pavlovian Cheapskates

claims.claim_text: For a premium product selling at $365, even a hundred-unit order ties up significant cash up front, which is why order sizes are stepped up only as confidence in the manufacturer grows.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like we're selling them for $365 now. So even just a hundred calendars, it's like, it's a lot of money up front from us
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Pricing into a very high margin bracket attracts knockoffs and outright counterfeits, which is a downside of positioning a product like fashion or design goods.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it gets to a significantly high level, then you start to have like knockoffs and you start to have true like outright fakes
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: A technically excellent FPGA system priced at $4,000 failed to sell, while a later $300 version of the same idea sold in far greater numbers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the $4,000 board didn't sell. So they eventually came out with a $300 version, which sold, which sold a lot better.
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: A vapor-phase soldering machine was positioned at 5,000 euros against roughly 10,000 euros for existing machines; the original 1,500-dollar hobbyist target was abandoned because required features would not fit that price.
claims.quote_verbatim: you said it was 10k euros to get any other machine so it's 5 000 europe's for the for the current machine
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Vapor Phase with Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: A cost multiplier of roughly 4x hardware cost is only a starting guideline; the actual price should be found by moving it until revenue against unit volume is maximized, and that optimum shifts with market conditions such as a recession.
claims.quote_verbatim: we always talk about like 4X, the hardware cost is like, is like a guideline
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fan Fanboys

claims.claim_text: A product line spanning roughly $100 to $10,000 lets one company serve students, researchers and professional security evaluators from the same portfolio.
claims.quote_verbatim: a hundred bucks to 10,000 or something like that for products that people could buy
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: When component costs such as memory are rising, one board vendor limits price revisions to no more than once per quarter to keep pricing predictable for customers.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've committed to not doing pricing updates more than once a quarter.
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Chronic underpricing comes from costing only the parts and ignoring the labor of making the thing; a hundred-dollar service was later tiered at $150 for the first hundred individual customers and $300 for institutional buyers or later orders.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first hundred customers get it for $150. So we only actually, for individuals, the price only went up by $50. But for universities or like companies that need an invoice or after the first hundred chips are sold, then it goes up to $300.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Embedding a price point in the company or product name removes your ability to raise the price later, so keep the name independent of the number.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have like enough business sense to know not to embed the price into the name of the company
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Engineers systematically underprice by reasoning from parts cost, when the correct question is what a buyer will actually pay for the finished object; a kit with about three dollars of parts sold fine at twenty dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: is someone willing to pay $20 for a knickknack? And yes, they are.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fan Fanboys

attribution_notes: Speaker labels in this bundle are unreliable in both directions; where the transcript label contradicted the content I attributed by content and recorded it here.
ep=101 header labels Chris Gammell, but the words describe the speaker's own company's product tiers and hobbyist offerings — attributed to Matt Ettus.
ep=105 both claims are the guest describing his own transparent pricing formula — attributed to Chris Anderson.
ep=159 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the content is a consultant recounting his own engagements with a diagnostics company and heavy-industrial clients — attributed to Eric Ries.
ep=189 header labels Chris Gammell, but the speaker describes running a reseller business competing on commodity prices — attributed to Marcus Schappi.
ep=235 speaker describes the pricing policy of the organization he works for — attributed to Matt Richardson.
ep=250 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the price-raise from $100 to $185 after fulfillment is the guest's own campaign — attributed to Vic Aprea.
ep=325 header labels differ across the two passages; both quoted lines describe the guest's own camera and reward-tier strategy — attributed to David Kronstein.
ep=544 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the surrounding lines address the speaker by name in reply, indicating the price-band judgment is the guest's — attributed to Pete Staples.
ep=593 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the $4,000-to-$300 board history is recounted by the guest — attributed to Ben Jordan.
ep=50, 58, 59, 71, 221, 259, 260, 314 left as null: these are rapid host-to-host exchanges where the quoted sentence could belong to either voice and no content cue resolves it.
ep=368 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE but the content is unambiguously the meter designer describing his own product history - attributed to Dave Jones.
